newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia speeds recognition of opposition victories.
newsitem.headline: Serbia speeds recognition of opposition victories.

text.p: Serbia's autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic lost no time in pushing through a new law recognising his opponents' victories in local elections after three months of domestic protests and foreign pressure.

While demonstrators continued to gather in Belgrade's streets to demand Milosevic reinstate municipal poll results in 14 towns and cities, the official news agency Tanjug reported that his government had approved a draft law which parliament would consider in extraordinary session next Tuesday.
Serbia's three-party Together or Zajedno coalition, students and professional groups, from laywers to actors, have braved police baton charges to demand democratic reforms.

Their central demand, endorsed by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, has been reinstatement of local election victories annulled by Milosevic's ruling socialists on grounds of unspecified "irregularities".
Officially, at least, it was overseas pressure that persuaded the socialist establishment to back down.

Quoting the Serbian Information Ministry, Tanjug said the government accepted that Serbia's relations with the OSCE and international community generally outweighed the importance of any electoral dispute.
Milosevic had suddenly announced on Tuesday that he was asking parliament to reinstate the results.

On Sunday he had ordered his anti-riot police to forcibly break up the demonstrations. Successive baton charges left scores injured in the worst violence seen in Belgrade for years and this prompted a renewed international outcry.

While municipal bodies have few real powers, they do control regional media, especially television and radio. Other opposition demands have included a free press and independent judiciary ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections due by the end of this year.

Deeply in debt, its industry devastated by international sanctions imposed for Belgrade's role in fomenting Serb rebellions in Croatia and Bosnia, Serbia faces declining living standards for most of its 10 million people.
Based on official statistics, economists say 26.5 percent of the work force have no jobs, but unofficial calculations suggest half are out of work.

While diplomats have wondered why Milosevic took three months to respond to opposition demands, authoritative sources in Belgrade said it took time for pragmatists to prevail over diehards within the socialist establishment.

The draft law, read out on radio and television and carried by Tanjug, declares as final the provisional (and disputed) results of November's polls, clearly listing the councils in the 14 towns and cities, including Belgrade.
It says the law comes into force the day after its publication in the official state gazette.
